title: AI Adoption Among Legal Professionals Has More Than Doubled in a Year, New 8am Report Finds, But Firms Lag Far Behind Individual Practitioners
author: Bob Ambrogi

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of useful task-level AI adoption constrained by institutional readiness, and materially extends it with survey evidence that personal use and perceived productivity gains are advancing faster than firm implementation, training and governance. Its predominantly solo and small-firm sample and reliance on self-reports limit broader conclusions about measured capability or organisational value.
qs: ### **Firm-Level Adoption Lags**  Despite greater individual adoption, law firms as institutions are moving more slowly, the report concludes.
More than half of respondents (54%) said their firm has provided no training on the responsible use of AI and has no plans to do so.

st.t: AI adoption: Enthusiasm cannot establish investment value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s bounded account: it documents substantial optimism despite governance and preparedness concerns, while presenting staffing effects as conflicting expectations rather than observed outcomes. It does not provide evidence that enthusiasm establishes investment value or realised transformation.
qs: **Despite concerns around governance and preparedness, most legal professionals expressed optimism about AI’s long-term impact on the profession.

st.t: Firm adoption: Access outruns dependable integration
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition that rapid individual uptake has outpaced dependable firm-wide integration. It contrasts 69% individual use with 46% firm implementation and reports widespread gaps in policies, training and preparedness. Its productivity, billing, staffing and ROI findings are self-reported benefits or expectations rather than evidence of realised firm-wide transformation or commercial value.
qs: This year, it stands at 69%, meaning adoption more than doubled in the span of a single year.
Only 46% of firms say they have implemented general-purpose AI tools, although that figure rises to 58% among firms with more than 20 lawyers.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The survey supports the cluster’s calibrated position: respondents expect AI to expand access through routine-task automation and self-help resources, but regard legal-aid funding, court modernisation and procedural simplification as substantially higher priorities. Its evidence is self-reported and predictive, and it does not directly assess verification risks or whether increased access produces effective remedies.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster by documenting rapid use of AI for bounded research, drafting and summarisation tasks, alongside self-reported productivity gains and substantial institutional gaps in training, policy and preparedness. Its evidence supports workflow reconfiguration and competence-risk concerns, while appropriately treating billing and workforce effects as respondent expectations rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: Among those personally using gen AI, 38% said they save one to five hours per week, 14% reported saving six to 10 hours weekly, 5% reported saving 11 to 15 hours, and 4% reported saving 16 or more hours per week.
More than half of respondents (54%) said their firm has provided no training on the responsible use of AI and has no plans to do so.

st.t: Research representation: Purposeful samples limit wider claims
st.an: The source supports the cluster by documenting the survey population’s age, geography, experience, practice-area and gender composition. These descriptive characteristics provide necessary context for interpreting whom the survey represents, without establishing national representativeness or profession-wide AI effects.
qs: Geographically, 53% of respondents were based in urban areas, 37% in suburban settings, and 10% in rural areas.
Most respondents (64%) were over the age of 40, while 12% were under 30.

kp.k: Individual generative AI adoption more than doubled
kp.d: The article reports 8am survey findings showing work-related use of general-purpose generative AI rising from 31% in 2025 to 69% in 2026, after standing at 27% in 2024. Use was frequent: 28% used it daily, 31% several times weekly, and 19% never used it; immigration practitioners had the highest reported daily use at 40%.
qs: In 2024, 27% of legal professionals reported using general-purpose gen AI tools for work. By 2025, that figure had risen to 31%. This year, it stands at 69%, meaning adoption more than doubled in the span of a single year.
Nearly one-third of respondents (28%) said they use gen AI every day, and another 31% use it several times a week. Only 19% reported never using gen AI tools.

Among immigration law practitioners, daily use reached 40%, which the report attributes to the high volume of repetitive document preparation, form automation and multilingual communication tasks common in that practice area.

kp.k: Drafting, research, brainstorming and summarization dominate use
kp.d: Among general-purpose AI users, the most common tasks were correspondence drafting and general research, both at 58%, followed by brainstorming at 54% and document summarization at 47%. Legal-specific AI, used by 42% of respondents, was led by legal research at 58%, document drafting at 49%, and summarization at 47%.
qs: Among those using general-purpose AI tools, the most common applications were for drafting correspondence (58%), general research (58%, up from 46% last year), brainstorming (54%), and summarizing documents (47%, up from 39% last year).

For legal-specific AI tools — used by 42% of respondents — the leading applications were legal research (58%), drafting documents (49%), summarizing documents (47%), drafting correspondence (43%), general research (43%), drafting document templates (38%), editing documents (36%), brainstorming (34%), knowledge management (20%), analyzing firm data (16%), creating training materials (13%) and generating marketing materials (12%).

kp.k: Practitioners report substantial productivity and quality benefits
kp.d: Among personal generative AI users, 38% reported saving one to five hours weekly, 14% six to 10 hours, 5% 11 to 15 hours, and 4% at least 16 hours. Separately, 33% said AI improved work quality without saving time, while only 6% reported no productivity benefit, down from 16% in the prior year.
qs: Among those personally using gen AI, 38% said they save one to five hours per week, 14% reported saving six to 10 hours weekly, 5% reported saving 11 to 15 hours, and 4% reported saving 16 or more hours per week.

Beyond raw time savings, 33% of respondents said AI improved the quality of their work even when it produced no efficiency gains in hours saved. Only 6% of those personally using AI reported no productivity benefits at all, a drop from 16% the prior year.

kp.k: Institutional adoption trails individual practitioner use
kp.d: Only 46% of firms reportedly implemented general-purpose AI, compared with 69% individual use; adoption rose to 58% among firms with more than 20 lawyers. Firm-level legal-specific AI adoption was 34%, up from 21% the year before but still below a majority.
qs: Despite greater individual adoption, law firms as institutions are moving more slowly, the report concludes.

Only 46% of firms say they have implemented general-purpose AI tools, although that figure rises to 58% among firms with more than 20 lawyers. Adoption of legal-specific AI tools at the firm level stands at 34% — an increase from 21% the year before, but still a minority of firms.

kp.k: Trusted software and legal expertise encourage firm adoption
kp.d: Firms adopting legal-specific AI most often cited its availability in trusted existing software (52%), provider understanding of workflows (47%) and ethical requirements (46%), and greater confidence in legal-specific outputs than in general-purpose alternatives (43%).
qs: For firms that have adopted legal-specific tools, the top reasons cited were: availability of AI functionality within trusted legal software already in use (52%), confidence that the provider understands the firm’s needs and workflows (47%), confidence that the provider understands the firm’s ethical requirements (46%), and greater trust in the outputs of legal-specific tools compared to general-purpose alternatives (43%).

kp.k: Security, ethics, privilege and trust impede adoption
kp.d: The leading significant barriers to firm-wide AI adoption were data security at 46%, ethical concerns at 42%, and both privilege concerns and lack of trust in results at 39%. Cost was less often a significant concern at 24%, although 40% considered it a moderate concern; lack of knowledge also declined as a significant challenge from 38% to 20%.
qs: Data security concerns were cited as a significant barrier by 46% of respondents, followed by ethical concerns (42%), privilege concerns and lack of trust in results (each 39%).
Notably, cost was a less prominent barrier, with only 24% citing it as a significant concern, though 40% called it a moderate one.
The share of respondents citing lack of knowledge as a significant challenge dropped from 38% to 20% year over year, while those saying it is not an issue at all rose from 25% to 41%.

kp.k: Training significantly lags widespread individual AI use
kp.d: A majority, 54%, said their firms offered no responsible-AI training and had no plans to do so. Mandatory firm-wide training and optional training were each reported by 11%, while 17% expected their firm to introduce training within 12 months.
qs: More than half of respondents (54%) said their firm has provided no training on the responsible use of AI and has no plans to do so.

Only 11% said mandatory training was provided for all staff, and another 11% said training was available but optional. Another 17% said their firm had no training currently but planned to add it within 12 months.

kp.k: Most firms lack actively enforced AI policies
kp.d: Forty-three percent said their firm had neither a formal AI policy nor plans for one, while 24% were developing a policy. Only 9% reported a written, actively enforced policy, and 10% reported an informal or inconsistently enforced policy.
qs: Forty-three percent of respondents said their firm has no formal policy governing AI use and no plans to create one. Another 24% said they are in the process of developing a policy.
Only 9% reported having a written and actively enforced AI policy, and another 10% reported an informal or inconsistently enforced policy.

kp.k: Paralegals lead firms’ stated AI training priorities
kp.d: Respondents most frequently identified paralegals as an AI-training priority at 39%, ahead of partners at 30% and associates at 26%. The report suggests partners’ priority over associates may reflect their institutional decision-making influence despite their work being more strategic and less repetitive.
qs: Paralegals were most frequently identified as a training priority (39%), followed by partners (30%) and associates (26%).

The report observes that prioritizing partners ahead of associates is noteworthy given that partner work is generally more strategic and less tied to the routine, repetitive tasks that AI is designed to streamline, suggesting the prioritization may reflect partners’ influence over firm-wide decision-making.

kp.k: Larger firms perceive stronger competitive pressure and ROI
kp.d: Overall, 39% felt no competitive pressure to match rivals’ AI adoption and 29% felt minimal pressure, but only 17% of respondents from firms with at least 21 lawyers reported no pressure. AI also ranked first for expected three-year technology ROI at 29% overall and 51% among firms of that size.
qs: Overall, 39% of respondents said they feel no pressure to keep up with competitors’ AI adoption, and 29% described the pressure as minimal. However, among firms with 21 or more lawyers, only 17% reported feeling no pressure at all — suggesting larger firms experience AI adoption as a more competitive dynamic.

When asked which legal technology investment is most likely to deliver the biggest return on investment over the next three years, AI tools ranked first at 29% overall. Among firms with 21 or more lawyers, that figure rose to 51%.

kp.k: Respondents anticipate billing changes but little client pressure
kp.d: Approximately 47% thought AI could affect law-firm billing: 25% anticipated fewer billable hours per matter and 22% greater use of fixed-fee or alternative arrangements. These remain expectations rather than observed changes; only 6% reported client requests for AI-related price reductions and 3% frequent requests for evidence of AI efficiency.
qs: With regard to AI’s potential impact on law firm billing models, nearly half of respondents (approximately 47%) said AI could affect billing practices. Of those, 25% anticipated a reduction in billable hours per matter, and 22% expected greater adoption of fixed-fee or alternative billing arrangements.
Only 6% of respondents said clients are requesting AI-related price reductions, and only 3% said clients frequently ask for proof of AI-driven efficiency.

kp.k: Most respondents remain optimistic but firms feel underprepared
kp.d: Fifty-four percent viewed AI’s long-term professional impact positively, including 23% who were very optimistic, while 20% were somewhat or very pessimistic. Organizational preparedness was weaker: only 19% described their firms as very prepared for the next five years, and 16% said they were not prepared.
qs: When asked how prepared their firms are to manage the changes AI may bring over the next five years, only 19% said their firm is “very prepared.” About one-third (35%) described their firm as “somewhat prepared,” while 16% said their firm is not prepared for an AI-enabled future.
Fifty-four percent reported a positive view (23% very optimistic, 31% somewhat optimistic), while 26% remained neutral. Thirteen percent were somewhat pessimistic and 7% were very pessimistic.

kp.k: Respondents predict role creation and workforce displacement
kp.d: These are respondent predictions, not measured employment changes. Forty-one percent expected new AI-specialist or legal-technologist roles, 39% predicted fewer paralegal or support positions, and 21% predicted fewer junior associates. Views were not uniform: 22% expected support roles to expand, while 18% anticipated more contract lawyers or ALSP reliance.
qs: On anticipated changes to firm structure, 41% of respondents expected new AI-specialist or legal technologist roles to be created, 39% predicted a reduction in paralegal or support roles, 23% expected no significant change, 22% predicted an expansion of paralegal or support roles, 21% anticipated a reduction in junior associate positions, and 18% expected greater reliance on contract lawyers or alternative legal service providers.

kp.k: Traditional reforms outrank AI for access to justice
kp.d: Respondents rated access-to-justice interventions such as legal-aid funding, court modernization and process simplification above AI. AI tools for lawyers were selected by 17% and consumer-facing AI by 13%, compared with 55% for expanded legal-aid and public-defender funding, 51% for court modernization, and 50% for simpler legal processes.
qs: Asked what would most improve access to justice, respondents pointed to expanded legal aid and public defender funding (55%), court modernization and efficiency initiatives (51%), simplification of legal processes (50%), increased civic and legal education (47%), greater availability of pro bono services (38%), alternative dispute resolution options (31%), AI tools for lawyers (17%), and AI tools for legal consumers (13%).

kp.k: AI’s access potential coexists with legal-system risks
kp.d: Seventy-six percent believed AI had potential to expand access to justice, though the stated “very high” and “high” categories accounted for 15% and 22%, respectively. Proposed mechanisms included automating document preparation, expanding self-help resources and remote services, streamlining courts, improving research and lowering costs; concerns included fabricated citations, untrained-user overreliance, unauthorized practice of law and bogus filings.
qs: Notably, a strong majority (76%) believe AI has the potential to expand access to justice in the future, with 15% saying it has “very high potential” and 22% saying “high potential.”

The leading ways AI could help, according to respondents, were automating routine legal tasks such as document preparation (53%), expanding access to self-help legal tools and resources (52%), increasing availability of remote and virtual services (51%), streamlining court procedures (47%), improving legal research and efficiency (48%), and reducing the costs of legal services (46%).

However, the report also showed some skepticism as to AI’s use in A2J, with respondents raising concerns about fake citations, overreliance on technology by untrained users, unauthorized practice of law, and courts being “clogged with bogus filings” created by generative AI tools.

kp.k: Survey composition limits broad market generalization
kp.d: The findings derive from more than 1,300 legal professionals surveyed from September 19 to October 18, 2025. The sample was concentrated in solo and very small firms: 45% were solo practitioners and 38% worked in firms with two to five lawyers; 47% of respondents were partners, 24% paralegals, and 12% administrative or support staff.
qs: The survey was conducted between Sept. 19 and Oct. 18, 2025, and included more than 1,300 legal professionals.
Nearly half of respondents identified as law firm partners (47%), followed by paralegals (24%) and administrative or support staff (12%).

Firm sizes skewed heavily toward solo and small practices: 45% were solo practitioners and 38% were from firms with two to five lawyers. Firms with 6–20 lawyers represented 12%, 21–50 lawyers represented 2%, and firms with 51 or more lawyers accounted for 3%.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ambrogi reports 8am’s findings that individual AI adoption has accelerated, users report productivity and quality benefits, and institutional adoption and governance lag. Survey respondents predict changes to billing, staffing and access to justice.
pts.d: The article attributes the findings to 8am’s 2026 Legal Industry Report, written by Nicole Black. Reported individual work use increased from 31% in the preceding report year to 69%; legal-specific tools are used by 42% of respondents. Uses include correspondence, research, brainstorming, document drafting and summarization. Among personal users, 38% report saving one to five hours weekly, 14% six to 10 hours, 5% 11 to 15 hours, and 4% at least 16 hours. Separately, 33% report improved work quality without time savings; only 6% of personal users report no productivity benefit. Firm implementation is lower: 46% for general-purpose tools and 34% for legal-specific tools. Security, ethics, privilege and distrust of results are reported barriers, while trusted existing software and providers’ perceived understanding of workflows and ethical requirements encourage adoption. Organizational preparation trails use: 54% report no responsible-use training and no plans for it, while 43% report no formal AI policy and no plans to create one. Respondents anticipate reduced billable hours and greater fixed-fee or alternative billing, although present client pressure is limited. Staffing expectations include new AI-specialist or legal technologist roles (41%), fewer paralegal or support roles (39%), more such roles (22%), fewer junior associates (21%), and greater reliance on contract lawyers or ALSPs (18%); 23% expect no significant structural change. AI ranks first among technologies expected to deliver the largest return on investment, selected by 29% overall. Respondents also see potential for AI to expand access to justice through automation, self-help resources, remote services, court efficiencies and lower costs, while expressing concerns about fabricated citations, untrained users’ overreliance, unauthorized practice and bogus filings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of a legal-technology company’s survey, year-over-year survey comparisons and respondents’ illustrative comments; future impacts are respondents’ expectations rather than measured outcomes.
pts.d: Ambrogi summarizes 8am’s report rather than presenting an independent experiment or benchmark. The survey included more than 1,300 legal professionals and was conducted September 19–October 18, 2025. Its sample is heavily concentrated in solo and very small firms: 45% solo practitioners and 38% firms with two to five lawyers. Partners account for 47%, paralegals 24%, and administrative or support staff 12%. Adoption, time savings, quality improvements, barriers and governance arrangements are self-reported. Respondent comments illustrate writing improvement, chronology generation, timekeeping and document management. Billing, staffing, return-on-investment and access-to-justice claims are survey forecasts or beliefs, not evidence that those changes have already occurred. The report’s explanation for immigration practitioners’ higher daily use connects it to repetitive document, form and multilingual tasks. Its suggestion that partners’ decision-making influence explains their training priority is an interpretation, not a separately demonstrated finding. The supplied article does not provide a sampling frame, response rate, weighting procedure or objective validation of reported productivity gains.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current-use findings reflect a late-2025 survey published as a 2026 report; explicit forecasts concern three-year investment returns and five-year preparedness, while most structural and access-to-justice predictions have no fixed deadline.
pts.d: The article describes adoption as 27% in 2024, 31% in 2025 and 69% 'this year'; the latest figure nevertheless derives from fieldwork in September–October 2025. Its claim of more than doubling therefore follows the article’s report-year comparison, not a survey conducted during 2026. Productivity benefits are expressed as weekly savings among personal AI users. Seventeen percent report plans to add training within 12 months. Return-on-investment expectations cover the next three years; preparedness concerns AI-related changes over the next five years. Billing and staffing forecasts and AI’s future access-to-justice potential lack a more specific horizon. The article says approximately 47% think AI could affect billing and then uses 'Of those' for the 25% anticipating fewer billable hours and 22% expecting more alternative billing; that wording should not be silently converted into an unambiguous whole-sample denominator. Expectations are qualified by dissent and uncertainty: 27% foresee minimal or no billing impact and 26% are unsure. AI’s access-to-justice potential is not presented as an achieved result, and respondents rank AI tools below funding, court modernization and process simplification as proposed improvements.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source distinguishes individual practitioners from firms, smaller from larger practices, different occupational roles, and legal clients and underserved members of the public.
pts.d: Individual legal professionals report changes in everyday research, writing and document work. Immigration practitioners report 40% daily use, which the report relates to their task mix. Firms face adoption, training and policy decisions; general-purpose implementation reaches 58% among firms with more than 20 lawyers. Larger firms report stronger competitive pressure and higher expectations of AI investment returns: 51% of respondents from firms with at least 21 lawyers select AI as the likely largest-return investment. These larger-firm findings concern a small segment of the sample, since only 5% come from firms with at least 21 lawyers. Paralegals, support staff and junior associates are subjects of predicted role reductions, although some respondents foresee support-role expansion. AI specialists and legal technologists are potential new roles, while contract lawyers and ALSPs may receive more work. Paralegals are the most frequently identified training priority (39%), ahead of partners (30%) and associates (26%). Clients may encounter changing prices and billing models, but few currently request AI-related discounts or evidence of efficiency. For access to justice, the prospective beneficiaries are people needing affordable legal assistance or self-help resources, not merely enterprise purchasers seeking savings; courts and untrained users are also exposed to the reported risks of faulty AI-generated legal material.
